prompt.context: A folding carton manufacturer has hired your consulting firm because it is facing declining profitability in its North American operations. The firm has two teams working for this client: one team is working on revenue sources, pricing, and customer relationships. Our team is focusing on operations — specifically the client's 10 plants in North America and what the client can do to cut costs.
prompt.question: What can you do to help the client cut costs and improve profitability in its North American operations?

clarifying_info.q: What is the biggest cost driver for the client?
clarifying_info.a: Raw materials (paper) are the biggest percentage of carton cost. Labor is a relatively small percentage of manufacturing cost.

clarifying_info.q: Is the manufacturing process labor-intensive or automated?
clarifying_info.a: The manufacturing process is almost completely automated. The client spends a lot of time on equipment setups.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client's capacity utilization compare with competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The client is not sure how its capacity utilization compares with competition.

clarifying_info.q: Has the competition made any recent operational changes?
clarifying_info.a: Competitors have not made any recent significant changes in operations.

clarifying_info.q: Where does the client source its raw materials?
clarifying_info.a: The client is a division of a bigger company and purchases its raw materials (paper) from another division at a transfer price that is greater than the market price.

clarifying_info.q: Are the plants run as cost centers or profit centers?
clarifying_info.a: The plants are run as profit centers.

framework: Start with the components of profitability: revenue and costs
Narrow to operations and cost reduction per interviewer guidance
Break costs into fixed (overhead, plant space, factory costs) and variable (raw materials, labor)
Identify biggest cost drivers: raw materials, capacity utilization, factory operations, distribution/supply chain, inventory
Examine business structure: profit-center vs. cost-center plants, number of plants (10) and rationale
Benchmark against competition on capacity utilization and factory operations
Assess transfer pricing policy for raw materials
Consider distribution and supply chain costs relative to competitors

questions.prompt: What are the main cost categories, and which is the biggest driver?
questions.guidance: Candidate should break costs into fixed (overhead, plant/factory costs) and variable (raw materials, labor). Should identify raw materials (paper) as the largest cost driver. Labor is a relatively small share. Should ask about the sourcing arrangement for paper.

questions.prompt: What is the impact of the transfer pricing policy on raw material costs?
questions.guidance: The client buys paper from a sister division at a transfer price above market price. This means the client's raw material cost is structurally higher than competitors who buy at market. The transfer pricing policy allows another division to profit but hurts this division's competitiveness. Candidate should recommend reexamining the transfer pricing policy — ideally allowing the division to source at market price, or at minimum reviewing whether the premium is justified.

questions.prompt: How should the client evaluate its plant capacity and factory operations?
questions.guidance: The client does not know how its capacity utilization compares with competitors. Candidate should recommend benchmarking capacity utilization against similar companies. The manufacturing process is highly automated but spends significant time on equipment setups — setup time is a lever to reduce. Candidate should ask whether batch sizes and setup time are optimized, and how they compare with competition.

questions.prompt: What are the implications of running each of the 10 plants as a profit center?
questions.guidance: Profit-center structure creates incentive for each plant to sell high-margin products and avoid low-margin ones. This may not align with the client's overall marketing and product-mix strategy. It is better to optimize all plant operations together rather than have each plant act independently. Candidate should weigh advantages (local accountability, motivation) vs. disadvantages (misalignment with corporate strategy, suboptimal product mix overall).

questions.prompt: Is operating 10 plants optimal? What are the tradeoffs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should question whether 10 plants is the right number. Plants close to customers or suppliers may reduce distribution/logistics costs. But fixed costs of operating each plant may outweigh proximity benefits. Should discuss tradeoffs of consolidating (closing some plants) vs. expanding. No definitive answer required — framing the tradeoff correctly is key.

brainstorming.prompt: What levers does the client have to reduce costs across its operations?

categories.name: Raw Materials
ideas: Renegotiate transfer pricing with sister division to buy paper at or near market price
Explore external market sourcing as leverage or alternative
Reduce paper waste in manufacturing process

categories.name: Plant Capacity & Utilization
ideas: Consider consolidating plants if fixed costs outweigh proximity benefits

categories.name: Factory Operations
ideas: Reduce equipment setup time (key lever given automated, setup-heavy process)
Optimize batch sizes to reduce changeovers
Implement lean manufacturing or continuous improvement programs
Review automation investments to further reduce labor share

categories.name: Organizational Structure
ideas: Convert plants from profit centers to cost centers to align incentives with overall strategy
Ensure product-mix decisions are made at divisional level, not plant level

categories.name: Distribution & Supply Chain
ideas: Analyze distribution costs relative to competitors
Evaluate whether plant locations minimize logistics costs
Optimize inventory levels to reduce carrying costs

recommendation: Focus immediately on the transfer pricing policy for paper — the biggest cost driver — and push to align internal transfer price with market price or allow external sourcing
Benchmark capacity utilization and equipment setup times against competitors to identify the largest operational gaps
Shift plants from profit centers to cost centers so product-mix decisions optimize total division profitability, not individual plant margins
Evaluate whether 10 plants is optimal and model the cost-benefit of consolidation
risks: Transfer pricing change may face resistance from the sister division and corporate leadership
Consolidating plants could disrupt customer relationships and increase distribution costs
Changing plant incentive structure requires change management and may reduce local accountability
next_steps: Commission a transfer pricing analysis comparing internal rate vs. market rate and quantify the cost disadvantage
Conduct a capacity utilization benchmarking study across all 10 plants versus industry peers
Model scenarios for plant consolidation (e.g., 10 → 7 or 8 plants) and compare fixed-cost savings vs. logistics cost increases
Pilot moving one or two plants to a cost-center model and measure impact on product mix and margins
